articles.text: Survey reveals reason for families who may leave school district Many families reluctantly pulled children from Piedmont schools this past year to enroll them in schools that are safely and successfully offering in-person instruction. Looking ahead to the 2021/22 school year, our family desperately wants to return to PUSD; however, we – and all families – need assurances that the district’s top priority is to reopen its schools for full-time in-person instruction for all grades in August. As more and more data show that schools can reopen safely with proper precautions, as all teachers in Piedmont will likely be offered COVID vaccines by this summer, and most importantly, as growing evidence has shown that long-term distance learning is doing real harm to our children, full-time in-person instruction is absolutely essential for the 21/22 school year. Without it, many families, like mine who left the district this year, will likely stay away, and many more will leave in the coming months. While I have been thrilled to see grades K-6 begin some in-person instruction over the last few weeks, the current hybrid schedules (ranging from 2-4 hours of weekly in-person instruction for secondary students to 9 hours for elementary) are simply not enough to make up for the social, emotional, and academic losses caused by one year of distance learning. Knowing that families soon need to make school decisions for next year (most private school deposits, for example, are due in March), I asked Piedmont School District to survey families about their intentions to stay in the district next year. Superintendent Booker declined the request. As a result, a group of parents conducted their own survey. It ran from February 2–14, with over 400 PUSD families participating. The results are telling: • Nearly 50% of the respondents (198 families) said they are very or somewhat likely to leave the district if the school year begins with hybrid instruction. These numbers are vastly different from the enrollment projections the school district released this week. It predicted that district enrollment will decline by only 54 students next year. • An additional 51 families said they are not in a position to leave the district if 2021/22 begins with hybrid instruction, but they would if they could. • More than 270 families who had previously donated to the Piedmont Education Foundation, representing 66% of all survey respondents, said they would reduce their annual donation or give nothing next year if Piedmont schools do not open for full-time in-person instruction. With this important data in hand, we call on Superintendent Booker and PUSD’s school board to demonstrate a firm commitment to reopening PUSD’s schools for full-time in-person instruction in August this year so that families are not forced to leave a school district that they want so much to be a part of. articles.text: What does the Bible say? One answer is: absolutely nothing. Maybe it’s the politics in the air and perhaps even in our drinking water, but whatever the source, it seems like there is a renewed desire to be on God’s side. The introductory phrase “the Bible says…” is back with a vengeance. But I can assure you that any sentence that begins with those words makes no sense whatsoever. That babbling Bible has told women to sit down and shut up, called science a tool of the devil and fueled anti-Semitism and racism. This theological ventriloquism has led people through valleys of guilt, shame and fear, no doubt to support the status quo and keep the powerful in power. This arrogant preface is defended with the argument that a true believer takes the word of God literally. But which word are we talking about? If we are talking about the actual words composed by the original authors of the books of the Bible then shouldn’t those who feel so strongly about the literal word only quote from the original language? Obviously the first thing to note is that the Bible is a translation in progress. For example, the Greek word for “sin” is the same word used in archery to describe an arrow that has simply missed its mark. articles.text: Americans have been paying attention to the Biden-Harris Administration’s climate actions as the unrelenting pace of climate change marches on. Former President Trump never took interest in pursuing extensive climate action, instead opting to reverse former executive actions and open up formerly inaccessible federal lands for fossil fuel extraction. The Trump Administration’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) was helmed by a fossil fuel magnate, and Trump consistently rolled back environmental progress, perhaps most famously when he withdrew the United States from the 2015 Paris Climate Accord. With the Biden-Harris administration in its early days, let’s take a look at what the president has done so far, what his plans are, and how he hopes to shape environmental policy. A few weeks into his term, most of President Biden’s significant policies have been overturning the executive actions that Trump enacted in office. President Biden has recommitted the U.S. to the Paris Climate Accord, cancelled the Keystone Pipeline, undone Trump’s rollback of automobile mileage requirements, and frozen a series of Trump’s executive actions related to air quality. While admirable, some of these executive actions could potentially get mired in court, leading to lost time on critical issues. Additionally, executive actions are fickle. They need to be reinforced by legislation, otherwise they can easily be negated by the following president. With full control of both congressional chambers until 2022, Democrats have a chance to pass environmental legislation that can impact decades of emissions. The new administration has signaled that climate actions will be tied to both infrastructure spending and jobs. Two-thirds of the buildings that exist today will still be here in 2050, showing how infrastructure actions we take now are incredibly important. Biden’s congressional representatives run the range of ideologies, with some asking for more progressive actions like the “Green New Deal,” while others call for caution and restraint moving forward. It will take bold action to guide party members and attain the votes necessary to actually pass bills. President Biden has called for numerous plans and goals related to climate action. This includes calling for 100 percent clean energy by 2035, a promise certain to raise eyebrows. Progressive California has only set a goal of 2045 for this metric, and achieving this on a national scale would require that no coal or gas-powered plants could exist in 14 years. Unlikely? Perhaps. But this kind of aggressive action is what is necessary to limit emissions. President Biden’s website says he will upgrade 4 million buildings before 2025, as well as provide direct cash rebates and financing to upgrade and electrify home appliances. Electrification is a priority here in Piedmont due to the direct impact it has on natural gas emissions. Biden wants to “spur the construction of 1.5 million sustainable homes”, although this sounds more open ended than the cash rebates promise. The overarching promise of the administration is to “build modern infrastructure.” We will have to wait to see what that means in practice, but it is an important next step towards increasing the nation’s sustainability efforts. Finally, the administration claims it will set new federal netzero standards for new commercial buildings by 2030. A good goal, but an earlier deadline could have an even greater impact. Perhaps most importantly, many of these goals suggest that the federal government will be focusing attention on climate and energy issues in a way that local and state governments have been shouldering over the last few years. In addition to Biden’s admirable promises, numerous areas of concern still remain. Fracking produces 69% of all oil and gas wells in America, helping make the U.S. the #1 producer of oil and natural gas in the world. Despite the numerous environmental issues surrounding the controversial drilling technique, Biden has made clear he does not want to ban it. Biden also has expressed no interest in reducing emissions stemming from the U.S. military, one of the largest emitters of GHG in the world. His plan for net zero GHG emissions by 2050 hinges on further developing carbon sequestration technology, a risky choice that has not been tested successfully at scale and is not guaranteed to succeed. Although Biden is far better than Trump on almost every climate metric, more actions will be required to stop the many negative effects of climate change. But rhetoric and intentions from highly visible people at the national level can have an important impact on attitudes. pages.text: Wednesday, February 24, 2021 3 News What a new administration means for federal climate action By Nate Redinbo Americans have been paying attention to the Biden-Harris Administration’s climate actions as the unrelenting pace of climate change marches on. Former President Trump never took interest in pursuing extensive climate action, instead opting to reverse former executive actions and open up formerly inaccessible federal lands for fossil fuel extraction. The Trump Administration’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) was helmed by a fossil fuel magnate, and Trump consistently rolled back environmental progress, perhaps most famously when he withdrew the United States from the 2015 Paris Climate Accord. With the Biden-Harris administration in its early days, let’s take a look at what the president has done so far, what his plans are, and how he hopes to shape environmental policy. A few weeks into his term, most of President Biden’s significant policies have been overturning the executive actions that Trump enacted in office. President Biden has recommitted the U.S. to the Paris Climate Accord, cancelled the Keystone Pipeline, undone Trump’s rollback of automobile mileage requirements, and frozen a series of Trump’s executive actions related to air quality. While admirable, some of these executive actions could potentially get mired in court, leading to lost time on critical issues. Additionally, executive actions are fickle. They need to be reinforced by legislation, otherwise they can easily be negated by the following president. With full control of both congressional chambers until 2022, Democrats have a chance to pass environmental legislation that can impact decades of emissions. The new administration has signaled that climate actions will be tied to both infrastructure spending and jobs. Two-thirds of the buildings that exist today will still be here in 2050, showing how infrastructure actions we take now are incredibly important. Biden’s congressional representatives run the range of ideologies, with some asking for more progressive actions like the “Green New Deal,” while others call for caution and restraint moving forward. It will take bold action to guide party members and attain the votes necessary to actually pass bills. President Biden has called for numerous plans and goals related to climate action. This includes calling for 100 percent clean energy by 2035, a promise certain to raise eyebrows. Progressive California has only set a goal of 2045 for this metric, and achieving this on a national scale would require that no coal or gas-powered plants could exist in 14 years. Unlikely? Perhaps. But this kind of aggressive action is what is necessary to limit emissions. President Biden’s website says he will upgrade 4 million buildings before 2025, as well as provide direct cash rebates and financing to upgrade and electrify home appliances. Electrification is a priority here in Piedmont due to the direct impact it has on natural gas emissions. Biden wants to “spur the construction of 1.5 million sustainable homes”, although this sounds more open ended than the cash rebates promise. The overarching promise of the administration is to “build modern infrastructure.” We will have to wait to see what that means in practice, but it is an important next step towards increasing the nation’s sustainability efforts. Finally, the administration claims it will set new federal netzero standards for new commercial buildings by 2030. A good goal, but an earlier deadline could have an even greater impact. Perhaps most importantly, many of these goals suggest that the federal government will be focusing attention on climate and energy issues in a way that local and state governments have been shouldering over the last few years. In addition to Biden’s admirable promises, numerous areas of concern still remain. Fracking produces 69% of all oil and gas wells in America, helping make the U.S. the #1 producer of oil and natural gas in the world. Despite the numerous environmental issues surrounding the controversial drilling technique, Biden has made clear he does not want to ban it. Biden also has expressed no interest in reducing emissions stemming from the U.S. military, one of the largest emitters of GHG in the world. His plan for net zero GHG emissions by 2050 hinges on further developing carbon sequestration technology, a risky choice that has not been tested successfully at scale and is not guaranteed to succeed. Although Biden is far better than Trump on almost every climate metric, more actions will be required to stop the many negative effects of climate change. But rhetoric and intentions from highly visible people at the national level can have an important impact on attitudes. Seventy-seven percent of American adults agree that we should be moving towards different energy sources than coal and gas, and 67 percent say the federal government is doing too little to reduce the effects of climate change. articles.text: At its meeting on February 11, the Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) discussed the results of its community engagement safer streets survey. The survey was open for approximately six weeks, from November 20, 2020 to January 3, 2021, and contained 19 questions. The city received 338 responses. According to the survey, residents noticed that walking and biking has increased throughout Piedmont throughout shelter-inplace orders – since March 2020. Survey respondents reported noticing that drivers “seem to be speeding more on main streets, such as Highland Avenue, Moraga Avenue, Grand Avenue, Oakland Avenue and Mountain Avenue.” Grand Avenue draws mixed feelings from survey respondents. Some felt that conditions for cyclists and pedestrians had improved but pointed to increased congestion and more traffic and speeding on adjacent streets. Almost all respondents reported noticing more people walking in the roadway due to social distancing requirements, and concern over lack of sidewalks in some areas. In response to the question of how the city could improve traffic and pedestrian safety, 162 offered suggestions. Ideas included reducing posted speed limits, having educational camResidents have expressed interest in a slow streets program in Piedmont. paigns to address speeding, and adding more pedestrian and bicycling infrastructure, such as speed bumps, wider sidewalks, lighted crosswalks, signage, and bike lanes. Respondents also suggested piloting a “slow streets” program, similar to programs Oakland and San Francisco have launched in response to shelter-in-place restrictions. Residents said that this would “calm traffic while encouraging more walking and biking.” The slow streets program in other Bay Area cities are designed to limit through traffic on certain residential streets, and allow them to be used as a shared space for people traveling by foot and bicycle – more common in Europe than the U.S. Residents also said that educating cyclists and pedestrians of all ages about safe use of streets, including encouraging people to walk on sidewalks, would improve traffic safety in Piedmont. The report found that there “is an appreciation for the increased number of stop signs” in Piedmont, especially on Magnolia Avenue and Hampton Road, as speeding continues to be a top concern. About 49 percent surveyed “strongly support” speed humps for certain residential streets. Only 9 percent of those surveyed said they strongly opposed speed humps. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s Schoolmates afterschool program is currently operating as Camp Smart Start and Play Pods. Both camps have served as the city’s distancelearning programs while schools in the district remain closed due to the ongoing health crisis. “Now that students are beginning to return to schools, these programs will be adjusted,” Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns said at a February 17 Recreation Commission meeting. Smart Start acted as the distance learning camp during traditional school hours, and Play Pods served as an afternoon camp from 2:30 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. Camp Smart Start originally followed the school district’s bell schedule for distance learning. Previously, groups were formed around age group or grade level, while still on a.m. and p.m. distance learning scheduling based on PUSD’s schedule. “It was challenging trying to coordinate two different schedules across 12 kids [a pod]. Going forward, in our new session, everyone is either on a morning schedule or an afternoon schedule,” he said. “This also means that we had to move around staff [schedules], to ensure that we had coverage at all sites. The good news is that with schools reopening, we’ve seen more parents who are interested in registering for the [afterschool] programs.” In the first session in January, 64 students were enrolled in Camp Smart Start and Play Pod programs. For the upcoming session, the Recreation Department is at maximum capacity of 72 students. “The fact that we are at capacity is a really good sign,” Stearns said. Stearns added that sign-up restrictions will likely be set in place for the foreseeable future. “We’re not going to go back to what Schoolmates looked like, pre-pandemic. In all likelihood, I don’t feel confident that we will go back to hourly registration, kids signing up the night before, or drop-ins. We’re not going to be able to be as flexible [in scheduling] as we used to be, but I’m hopeful that we will be able to offer more spots based on vaccinations and county guideline changes,” he said. The Piedmont Recreation Department is also hiring Recreation Leaders for its after-school program. Interested applicants may call the Department at 420- 3070, or contact Stearns at jstearns@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: The COVID experience has been hard for all of us, but especially hard for students. Every morning at exactly 8:30 a.m. we would log onto our computers and talk into the screen for over two hours. Even though we “see” all of our classmates regularly on the screen, it’s strange to think that we have not assembled as an in-person class this entire school year. I am excited to go back to school and see my classmates and teacher in 3D. Before the pandemic, I probably would have been excited to be behind a screen all day, but now that I’m actually doing that, I realize that in-person school is so much better. There were definitely times during the year when I thought going back to the actual classroom was a goal that was out of reach. Now that we have worked extra hard, stayed socially distant, worn our face masks even though we probably didn’t want to, we accomplished our goal. Thank you to everyone who helped make this happen, and especially to our teachers who have been there every step of the way! Sofia Meyer is a 5th grade student at Wildwood Elementary School.

articles.text: I recently received an email from a parent saying that it was time I “demand” teachers return to the classroom. This parent was livid that school isn’t open, and his anger was directed squarely at teachers. Apparently, he sees teachers as the only thing standing between him and a return to But this father isn’t alone in David Brooks, in his recent New York Times op-ed, entitled Children Need to Be Back in School Tomorrow (January 28, 2021), takes aim at teachers and suggests that teachers and their unions are willfully adding suffering to a year of national misery. Framing the issue of reopening schools in such simplistic terms – that it’s just about what teachers want – lends credence to a growing effort to blame teachHere’s what Brooks doesn’t understand – and what all parents need to know. The situation of reopening schools is complicated, and here’s what teachers would Kids and teachers gather together while exchanging ideas. tell you, if they could: Teachers would tell you that most school buildings are old, cramped, and poorly ventilated. No business or restaurant on the planet would be allowed to operate at full capacity in a setting as poorly designed as the average public school. Teachers would tell you that there isn’t enough room in the average school hallway to have students come and go at the same time safely without military-style precision. Teachers would tell you that the last people in the world who are capable of military-style precision are children, and that for the most part they simply can’t behave in advance of their developmental stage. This means children can’t not get squirrely, they can’t not be impulsive, they can’t not touch each other just for the fun of it. I supervised teenagers just last week and several of them inadvertently touched each other because they wanted to share something on their phones. Teachers spend every day with groups of children in schools, and as a result they know the limitations of school settings and childhood behavior better than anyone. Period. I encourage all parents to spend a moment thinking about one of your child’s favorite teachers, maybe the one who taught them to read, or to spell their name, or to do a geometry proof; the teacher who encouraged your child to stretch beyond what they thought was possible, and who praised them when they did. Imagine the teacher who wiped your child’s nose, hugged them when they fell in the playground, and taught them the beauty of poetry. Teachers want to return to schools. They want to be with your children. They want to return to the work that they love. They just want to be safe. That’s all. So, parents, please don’t be angry at teachers. They are not the enemy – they are your greatest ally. Teachers are the people who will be there for you and your children on the other side of this tragedy, to help pick up the pieces and heal. I know for a fact that teachers can’t wait to safely return to schools and do what they do best: help raise your children. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. This parent was livid that school isn’t open, and his anger was directed squarely at teachers. Apparently, he sees teachers as the only thing standing between him and a return to normal life. They are not. But this father isn’t alone in seeing teachers as the enemy. David Brooks, in his recent New York Times op-ed, entitled Children Need to Be Back in School Tomorrow (January 28, 2021), takes aim at teachers and suggests that teachers and their unions are willfully adding suffering to a year of national misery. Framing the issue of reopening schools in such simplistic terms – that it’s just about what teachers want – lends credence to a growing effort to blame teachers for our current situation. Here’s what Brooks doesn’t understand – and what all parents need to know. The situation of reopening schools is complicated, and here’s what teachers would As we return to school, thanks to our teachers By Sofia Meyer The COVID experience has been hard for all of us, but especially hard for students. Every morning at exactly 8:30 a.m. we would log onto our computers and talk into the screen for over two hours. Even though we “see” all of our classmates regularly on the screen, it’s strange to think that we have not assembled as an in-person class this entire school year. I am excited to go back to school and see my classmates and teacher in 3D. Before the pandemic, I probably would have been excited to be behind a screen all day, but now that I’m actually doing that, I realize that in-person school is so much better. There were definitely times during the year when I thought going back to the actual classroom was a goal that was out of reach. Now that we have worked extra hard, stayed socially distant, worn our face masks even though we probably didn’t want to, we accomplished our goal. Thank you to everyone who helped make this happen, and especially to our teachers who have been there every step of the way! Sofia Meyer is a 5th grade student at Wildwood Elementary School. This means children can’t not get squirrely, they can’t not be impulsive, they can’t not touch each other just for the fun of it. I supervised teenagers just last week and several of them inadvertently touched each other because they wanted to share something on their phones. Teachers spend every day with groups of children in schools, and as a result they know the limitations of school settings and childhood behavior better than anyone. Period. I encourage all parents to spend a moment thinking about one of your child’s favorite teachers, maybe the one who taught them to read, or to spell their name, or to do a geometry proof; the teacher who encouraged your child to stretch beyond what they thought was possible, and who praised them when they did. Imagine the teacher who wiped your child’s nose, hugged them when they fell in the playground, and taught them the beauty of poetry. Teachers want to return to schools. They want to be with your children. They want to return to the work that they love. They just want to be safe. That’s all. So, parents, please don’t be angry at teachers. They are not the enemy – they are your greatest ally. Teachers are the people who will be there for you and your children on the other side of this tragedy, to help pick up the pieces and heal. I know for a fact that teachers can’t wait to safely return to schools and do what they do best: help raise your children. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Council BSA tuned in this past Sunday to watch the national Be The Change event, where the inaugural class of female Eagle Scouts was showcased. Girls were welcomed into the Scouts BSA program, formerly Boy Scouts of America, in Spring 2019. The prestigious rank of Eagle Scout is the ultimate milestone of this program and girls have begun earning the rank of Eagle Scout. One of the members of the class, Kendall Jackson of Illinois, noted “My mom is a Scoutmaster, so I was just always around. Now that I am officially an Eagle Scout, I am ecstatic to be a part of something so historic and be a part of the first class. It’s never something I thought I would ever be able to do.” Though Piedmont did not have Eagle Scouts represented, Piedmont Scouts on Sunday watched the ceremony in awe. Mollie King of Piedmont’s Troop 4, said she was inspired by Kendall Jackson’s Eagle project, which involved conducting a workshop for high school seniors on financial responsibility and time management. “I thought this was really cool because I think a lot of people forget that Boy Scouts of America is about more than outdoor skills - it challenges youth to be bration made me feel like we are a part of something bigger and a part of something important. articles.text: La Coulée Verte and Bois de Vincennes The winter months are dwindling, but Paris restaurants, cafés, museums, theatres, department stores, and every imaginable entertainment remains closed. Worse, Paris may be experiencing a third wave of Covid-19 with the spreading United Kingdom mutant dubbed the UK-variant. France continues to enforce curfews and ban international travel with no end in sight, though England is predicting some normalcy by mid-May. For now, Paris parks are open, and as the days gently warm, there are greenbelt options to get some fresh air while practicing social distancing. Paris, though not ranked in the world as a green city, has more than 400 parks. Many agree the most admired are Luxembourg Gardens, Tuileries Garden at the Louvre, and Bois de Boulogne in the 16th arrondissement. Buttes-Chaumont at Belleville in the 19th district is an enchanting city park in the Luxembourg style but with a more intimate aura as a country place. Plus, it’s generally not as crowded with tourists. Jardin des Serres d’Auteil is a secret garden of greenhouse exotics at the southern tip of Bois de Boulogne. The Jardin des Plantes, the city’s vast botanical garden whose roots took hold for apothecary herbs to treat the Renaissance royals, is a top choice. On its grounds are the National Natural History Museum and academies for botany, mineralogy, and geology, while the gardens and natural history museum are a magnet for energetic children on school tours. La Coulée Verte, from the Bastille to Bois de Vincennes A high line park was built atop an obsolete railway spur from the Place de la Bastille to Bois de Vincennes, and since its opening in 1993 is a popular greenway. If the idea of converting an elevated Path along Coulée Verte where an obsolete train track used to be. Aligre market between Bastille and Nation plazas is a good place to pick up fresh produce, meat, fish, deli, and charcuterie before trail walking or afterwards to carry home for dinner. train line into a parkway seems familiar, the New York City High Line was inspired by the Paris trail and opened in 2007, running from the meatpacking district to 34th Street. The stairway entrance to this Paris elevated parkway is at the back of the Opéra Bastille along Rue de Lyon. The park, called the “green river”, is not an exact translation of La Coulée Verte. And earlier moniker was Promenade Plantée (the planted promenade). The walkway is a mile and a half of easy strolling through an assorted green trail of paths laden with roses, plantings, and flower gardens, wild greenery, a short canal. At varying locations, it branches into wider spaces with bench seating. Further along, the pathway narrows over the Jardin de Reuilly and snakes downhill to street level for bicyclists and walkers who will arrive at the entry to Bois de Vincennes in another mile and a half. Trail walkers may wish to bring food and drinks on sunny days and choose a scenic spot to picnic at Reuilly park. A favorite Bastille location, Marché d’Aligre with open stalls and covered counters stacked with produce and fresh foods, is open six days a week. A lot of the trail fun is the sheer elevation – walking on a raised platform places you eye to eye with the third or fourth level of buildings. One is peering over the railings at street intersections and gazing at apartments with glimpses of balconies and people walking below: it’s an urban adventure. The Opéra Bastille that opened to grand fanfare in 1989 was built on the spot that Gare de la Bastille occupied from 1859 to 1969. This second opera house designed for the Paris general populace is immense in size, holding: 2,745 seats; a 500-seat amphitheatre; a 230-seat studio theatre; set and costumes workshops; rehearsal rooms; and offices. Controversy has dogged the project including criticism about “disappointing” acoustics. Once you reach Reuilly, it’s decision-time with a half dozen options. From here you can take the stairs to street level to the Viaduc des Artes and stroll by workshops, cottage businesses, cafés, and retailers along Avenue Daumesnil, where the walk returns strollers to the Bastille. More options open when you decide to walk the entire Coulée Verte and reach the Bois de Vincennes. One may alternately catch the 46 bus on Avenue Daumesnil headed south and ride the mile and a half to the park. Vincennes is the largest park in Paris with crisscrossing foot trails clocking some 50 miles in length. Bicycle trails are also abundant. At the entry to Vincennes, Palais-Porte Dorée is an intriguing museum full of curiosities from the time of the French Colonial Exhibition in 1931, and a glorious example of the Art Deco age. Inside the park is a zoo that children love. Lac Daumesnil along Avenue Daumesnil is the park’s largest lake and entertains patrons with rentals of rowboats, bicycles, and pony rides around the lake for kids. Parc Floral is the site for international flower shows and filled with beauty when the tulips and daffodils are in bloom. From Parc Floral and across Lac des Minimes is a tropical plant garden. The 19th C. Paris Age of Parks Each of the 20 Paris districts was reconfigured with charming park-squares during the reign of Emperor Louis-Napoléon III, when he tasked his city manager Georges-Eugène Haussmann to Promenade Plantée, or Coulée Verte, view of the elevated train now a park in Paris 12th district and below the street-level shops known as Viaduc des Artes. Viaduc des Artes has workshops and artsy shops under the red brick arches below the Coulée Verte high line. Gare de la Bastille, about 1900. The railroad spur to Bois de Vincennes ended in 1969.

articles.text: the château is in its 10th century and is open as an attraction to tour the chapel commissioned by Saint Louis in the 13th C. and the donjon completed in 1380. This donjon is a heavily fortified tower standing 170 feet tall and built within the medieval fortress. The tower’s walls are six-feet thick; surrounded by a moat, along with gunports, impenetrable wooden The Parc-Zoologique at Bois de Vicennes is a popular option for children. doors, and iron-bar latches. The donjon was where the Royals took refuge once the castle walls were breached by the enemy as a last chance to survive. The Vincennes military training field was decommissioned shortly after World War II. Lucky for the future, when Louis-Napoléon III granted the forests of Boulogne and Vincennes in 1855, the sites were professionally designed in the early Victorian style, a romantic vision that still works for today’s visitors. The two parks are legendary, conceived with artistry and imagination. The latest 19th C. scientific methods were applied to construct lakes and drainage systems; roads and foot trails; and install flora and tree plantings of species numbering in the thousands. Each park has a hippodrome for horse racing, and Vincennes has a zoo. articles.text: Members of the PHS mountain bike team practice riding the Long Course of the Piedmont MTB Classic. Piedmont High School’s mountain bike team will host its first Piedmont MTB Classic race in March. Registration is now open. All proceeds will support the team, which is a club sport with no financial support from the high school. The event will take place over two weeks, March 7-21, so that riders can independently participate in the equivalent of time trials. Each participant will record his or her time on designated trail segments using the Strava app, and prizes will be awarded for the fastest riders in four categories: • Middle School • High School • Adult • Overall There are two options for each race, Short Course and the Long Course. The short course covers roughly 9 miles of trail with an elevation gain of approximately 900 feet. The Long Course is 15 miles with 2,500 feet of elevation gain. The cost to participate is $40. Race proceeds will be used to purchase a team trailer to help transport equipment to races. It will be dedicated to Lynden McLaughlan, a team coach who passed away unexpectedly in 2019. To sign up for the Classic and learn more about the race and the team, go to www.Piedmontmtb.com.

In Piedmont, this pushes sports like lacrosse, baseball, softball, and football into midMarch, while soccer and water polo aren’t likely to start until after April 19. For football, this comes after the sport was considered an Orange Tier athletics event, clearing the way for North Coast Section schools to complete their seasons by April 17. They will have a five-game season from March 19 to April 16, meaning there will be no post-season. “They’ve been hard-pressed to have a five-game season. We’re excited about that and anything else is just gravy. We’d just appreciate a heads up to get prepared for the appropriate plan,” said PHS football coach Jerome Johnson. Football is set to get its season underway the week of Friday, March 19 with a home game against Castro Valley. They will need to accomplish at least 14 days of practice before competing in a game. Athletes must have 10 individual days of practice in order to play – a far cry from the usual summer-long offseason festivities. The issue, however, comes with COVID-19 testing. Football and water polo will require weekly virus screenings. This means that football programs throughout the state, with extensive groups of volunteer coaches, must find a way to get tested and remain safe. “There are a lot of volunteers that need to be considered in the process… Outside the scope of the district, I’d like everyone to know that we have volunteers coming in who are extremely dedicated with a non-salary position to coach. We’d like to have more input and have our state officials be more considerate of our time,” added Johnson. Smet affirms that testing will be provided by the state, but the school is waiting for a solid commitment in writing from the California Department of Public Health. “The kids and coaches will have to be tested weekly for football and water polo. Testing will be paid for by the California Department of Public Health. However, we haven’t gotten an official confirmation from the state yet on how we are facilitating testing. Are we paying for it and getting reimbursed? We’re still waiting to find out,” he added. Another issue is the schedule of practices. Lacrosse, for instance, has yet to begin full-speed, game-simulation style practices. “It’s my understanding that March 1 is the magic date for full-on contact practices. Up to this point we’ve done very non-contact and very non-defense drills. We want to make sure this feels right. We’ve really only had four days where we’ve been allowed to pass,” said Piedmont girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan. articles.text: Saying Tottenham and manager Jose Mourinho are in hot water may be a bit of an understatement. Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players will present a concert this Sunday, February 28, featuring legendary violinist Dmitry Sitkovetsky and his work with the Sphinx Orchestra. The virtual concert will feature a rare personal exploration of his career, including his work as a soloist and as founder of the New European Strings Orchestra. Sitkovetsky has worked closely with Sphinx Orchestra founder Aaron Dworkin to mentor emerging musicians. The Sphinx Orchestra is a Detroit-based national organization dedicated to transforming lives through the power of diversity in the arts. Stikovetsky has selected two of the musicians to perform for Gold Coast Chamber audiences. This weekend’s performance includes Xavier Foley (double bass) and Sterling Elliot (cello). The program includes music by Ceasar Franck, Luigi Dallapiccola, Bach, Foley, and Rouhollah Khaleghi. Sitkovetsky, a resident of New York City and London, appeared in a solo concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on September 15, 2019. The concert will be streamed live via YouTube live at 4 p.m. on Sunday, February 28. The concert link will remain active for one week following the performance date. A Zoom after-party will take place, and Elliott and Foley will join patrons to answer questions and socialize. articles.text: San Francisco Opera House San Francisco Opera is slowly but surely signaling a return to live performances. It recently announced plans for 11 “drive-in” performances this spring season. Tickets will go on sale starting March 23. Live performances will begin with a new adaption of Rossini’s The Barber of Seville, starting April 23. It will be performed without intermission, and sung in English, with performances at the Marin Center in San Rafael. The opera also will have three performances of “The Adlers: Live at the Drive-In,” a recital by the Adler Fellow resident artists, which will be held in the open-air. In addition to its spring season, San Francisco Opera has announced it will be offering more digital content, including its “Opera is On” archive streaming series. SF Opera also is launching a series called “In Song” – 10-minute video profiles of six singers well-known to San Francisco audiences. Another series, “Atrium Sessions,” will have art songs and arias recorded in performance at the Atrium Theater. A new behind-thescenes podcast will complement the opera’s digital offerings. To purchase tickets to drive-in operas, or browse San Francisco Opera’s digital resources, visit https://sfopera.com/on-stage/.

It’s an easygoing, amiable crime comedy, of sorts – not laugh-out-loud comedy but filled with moments that create a long-lasting smile because of its sheer enjoyment. Redford portrays Forrest Tucker, a fedora-wearing oldster who happens to be a bank robber (and a prison escape artist). Every frame of the film, set in the early 1980s, has an old-timey feel to it, most shot in soft sepia tones. The look of it is a perfect fit for Redford and cast. Robert Redford and Sissy Spacek star in The Old Man & The Gun. The film opens in a small town inside a small bank. Forest walks up to the manager and with a smile explains that he’s not there for a loan or to make a deposit. He’s there to rob the bank. Flashing his gun in his waistband, he asks politely, still smiling, for the cash on hand. He is so pleasant, so gentlemanly that those he robs describe him in endearing terms. Getting what must be his second or third wind, Forrest cuts a crime-spree bank-heist swath across the Southwest. Clearly, he feels more alive than anything else and more himself when strolling into and then out of a bank with an old, worn briefcase full of teller cash. On his way home from one such “job” he stops to help a woman, Jewel (Sissy Spacek), who is having car trouble. Offering her a ride home, they make a stop for a cup of coffee. And, like everyone else that Forrest meets, she takes a liking to him. Ditto detective John Hunt (Casey Affleck), who is determined to catch up with not only Forrest but with his two partners in crime (Danny Glover and Tom Waits). What makes this film exceptional is how it allows the audience to be completely on Forrest’s side. As well, the small ember of a romance between Jewel and Forrest rings true – from their first coffee shop chat and then, later, when he tells her he’s a bank robber. She laughs and says something to the effect, “Yeah, right.” Perhaps she believes him; however, he is genuinely likable and good company. Redford is now age 82. In this role he aces Forrest Tucker like he’s slipping into a much-washed flannel shirt. It’s not a stretch for Redford to inhabit this sly old guy whose face is deeply lined but filled with good intentions. As Forrest, he exudes style and integrity. Clearly, it’s not about the money. As well, the movie is filled with small moments. One scene I found so very charming was when there was a quick cut from Forest being chased by the police to three kids with an old paint Robert Redford protrays bank robber Forrest Tucker in The Old Man & The Gun. can, painting a fence, just around the corner from the bank. Then it was back to the cops and Forrest. Just great stuff and confident filmmaking. Bottom line, it’s Redford and Spacek who create the unadorned delight of this film. They react to one another with warmth and caring, leavened by years of life experience, conveying their characters’ hidden loss, absent even a hint of the maudlin. If this is truly Redford’s adios, then he has chosen a small gem of a film to frame his exit. So nice. But I do hope he reconsiders. The Old Man & the Gun. Directed by David Lowry. Starring Robert Redford, Sissy Spacek, Casey Affleck and Danny Glover. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: The story of a Russian Mouse lost in the U.S. A scene from An American Tail. Movie review by Chris Honoré An American Tail, directed by Don Bluth, was the second feature by the Bluth studio, following The Secret of Nimh. Like NIMH, it’s a wonderfully animated adventure film, layered with award-wining songs and focused on a 7-year-old mouse named Fievel Mousekewitz. The year is 1885, and Fievel’s journey begins in Russia where his family – Papa Mouskevitz (Nehemiah Persoff), Mama Mousekevitz (Patricia Vohn), and Tanya Mousekevitz (Amy Green) – is attacked by Cossacks and cats and their home burned down. Fleeing Russia, they managed to board a tramp steamer on its way to America, where they believe there are no cats. During a thunderstorm, Fievel is separated from his family and washed overboard. His family is distraught, believing that Fievel is lost forever. Actually, remarkably, he is safely ensconced in a bottle, and washes up in the harbor of New York City where his quest to find his parents begins. Little Fievel is a stranger in a strange land, feeling very alone in a teeming city of tenements, yet determined to find his mother and father and sister. Safely on the dock, he firsts meets a French pigeon, Henri (Christopher Plummer), who takes him under his wing, so to speak. But he is only the first in what will be a rich cast of characters from a variety of countries. What he quickly learns is that there are indeed cats in America and one is named Tiger (Dom DeLuise) who befriends him. But there are also conniving rats, one called Warren T. (John Finnegan) who actually taking Fievel to a sweat shop where he is forced to work until he manages to escape with the help of an Italian mouse, Tony Toponi (Pat Musik). And so the quest continues. Fievel runs into the Mott Street Maulers, a take no prisoners gang of cats. In conflict with them is Gussie Mouseheimer (Madeline Kahn),a rich and domineering mouse. Meanwhile, Fievel’s parents grieve for their small son, convinced he couldn’t possibly have survived; however, it is only Tanya who insists that her brother is alive, telling her parents that she can feel it. The plot is a bit convoluted (perhaps busy is a better word) as Fievel makes his way from one close call to the next, with cat chases galore, always pushing forward, ever convinced that he will soon be reunited with his family. An American Tail is a compelling, at times a softly harrowing adventure, one that will capture the attention of a young audience who will be captured by the escapades of a small Russian mouse. An American Tail (1986). Animation. Directed by Don Bluth. With the voices of Philip Glasser, Dom DeLuise and Amy Green. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated G.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The Red Turtle is a breathtaking fable, written and animated by Oscar-winning Dutch filmmaker Michael Dudok de Wit in 2016, working in collaboration with Studio Ghibli, the renowned Japanese house of animation perhaps best known for creating the feature Ponyo. Note that though The Red Turtle has a PG rating and is only 80 minutes long, it is not simply kid friendly. What gives this film its emotional power is that not a single word is spoken, nor is a single word needed. In fact, the silence of the film falls away as the filmgoer is transported into a captivating story that is completely unexpected, one that gives the illusion of being slight but is instead deeply complex and almost Zen-like in its composition. The film opens with a raging, storm-tossed sea and abruptly the head of a man appears floating just above the surface, struggling to survive. He spots a capsized lifeboat and clings to it as the wind howls and the water churns. When the sun rises, the sky now clear, the man is lying on a wide sandy beach. He doesn’t stir until a small sand crab crawls up the leg of his pants and bites him. It’s then that he wakes, slowly stands, and looks around. He is alone. All he sees is ocean and a necklace of sand, finally noticing that just beyond the beach is a forest of lush green bamboo that covers the island. He searches the interior of the island and finds a fresh water lagoon in the interior. There is also fruit within reach. Following in his footsteps near the ocean’s edge is a small chorus of curious sand crabs. Days pass. The night sky is awash with stars and a soft crescent moon. Gradually the reality of his circumstances is revealed. His isolation is total. One day he imagines there is a string quartet playing on the beach. Determined to escape, using the bamboo from the forest, he builds a raft. But he barely gets beyond the breakwater sandbar when something hits his raft from below and shatters it. He is mystified, but he tries again. After more days of hard work using the plentiful bamboo, he launches into the ocean. Again, the raft is wrecked just beyond the shore. It is then that an enormous turtle with a bright red shell emerges from the deep. This time when he swims back the turtle follows, crawling awkwardly up onto the sandy beach. Angry and wracked by loneliness, his plan to escape once again ruined, he turns the massive turtle upside down and leaves it in the hot sun. What happens next is magical and I am reluctant to explain more. But suffice it to say that it is then that the narrative arc of the film is revealed. It invites the audience to step into a reverie that is so quietly offered up it can only be called a meditation on life. With a palette of vibrant and muted colors by the animators, it is all but impossible not to be drawn in, pulled, like a gentle out-going tide swirling around your ankles, the sand slipping from under your feet. The Red Turtle is a parable, in parts allegorical and archetypal, filled with moments that are profoundly moving. What is real and what is surreal is left courageously unanswered. And all that takes place as the film unfolds will linger, nudging the filmgoer to ponder its minimalist poignancy and its utter beauty. This film is the antidote to the cacophony of so many movies made for a younger demographic. But its depth, its silence, may be a bridge too far for some young viewers; it may require a patience beyond their reach. In contrast, adults will likely find The Red Turtle to be a universal story, its artistry incomparable, its humanity evocative and deeply moving. The Red Turtle (La Tortue Rouge, 2016). Animation. Directed by Michael Dudok de Wit. Produced by Studio Ghibli. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated PG. Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! articles.text: Russia is in the news a lot these days. Depending on your socio-political outlook, the slant could be favorable or unfavorable. When I was in Russia a few years ago I noticed that the people maintained a negative outlook on just about everything. They were very quick to say “nyet” despite ample evidence to the contrary. The restaurants served a wide variety of Russian food. Everything was prepared to order, and portions were large. Your food arrived at the table when it was prepared. This meant that everything arrived at different times. Dining could be a very lengthy affair; sometimes lasting about two hours. There are not many Russian restaurants in the United States. So, when I saw the Kolobok Russian food truck in Rocky’s Market parking lot on Leimert Blvd. two weeks ago, I said to myself: “let me try some of the things.“ I engaged the owner in conversation and found out she was from Piedmont. Who could have known? I selected some dessert crepes. I enjoyed my conversation with the owner and was delighted with the crepes. Kolobok later announced a special dinner for Valentine’s Day. That was all I needed. They offered a set menu and it was sumptuous, to put it mildly. My wife and I ordered two dinners. One was a salmon fillet enveloped by a flaky pastry. The English would be tempted to claim it in the name of Wellington because it is a fish version of Beef Wellington. Not since the days of the old Stagecoach restaurant in downtown San Francisco have I had anything this good. Preparing a Wellington is a very tricky thing and this one was done to perfection. The flaky pastry was perfectly browned. Other ingredients were included which only increased the delectability. The other main course was a large lamb shank braised in Georgian wine and fragrant root vegetables. The meat was delectable and ever so tender. To accompany these main courses were salads which included some smoked salmon. Even though it was a dinner for two, there was enough food to feed at least six. In considering how many people the meal could feed, the price was unbelievably low. Only one thing was missing: It was a take-out meal rather than dining in an elegant imperial dining room. It wasn’t a problem, however. We brought the food home, set the table with some nice China and poured a glass of red wine. Memories of my childhood returned when I saw that Kolobok offers stuffed cabbage. Their version was similar to what my grandmother made. My grandmother’s stuffing was entirely beef and Kolobok’s is a mixture of different meats. For quality, quantity, convenience, and price, Kolobok is a very good bet. Oh, I forgot to tell you… Kolobok is named for Russia’s national fairytale. The character is similar to the gingerbread man. I created my own version. In my version Kolobok is a cute little gourmet who ventures into the forest gathering rare and expensive mushrooms and forest berries. Instead of being eaten by the sly fox, Kolobok prepares a sumptuous dinner for his friends. What could be better? For a future treat, contact Ellen Doren, owner of Kolobok, at kolobokfood@gmail.com. Kolobok: Russia at its best By Joseph Gold Russia is in the news a lot these days. Depending on your socio-political outlook, the slant could be favorable or unfavorable. When I was in Russia a few years ago I noticed that the people maintained a negative outlook on just about everything. They were very quick to say “nyet” despite ample evidence to the contrary. The restaurants served a wide variety of Russian food. Everything was prepared to order, and portions were large. Your food arrived at the table when it was prepared. This meant that everything arrived at different times. Dining could be a very lengthy affair; sometimes lasting about two hours. There are not many Russian restaurants in the United States. So, when I saw the Kolobok Russian food truck in Rocky’s Market parking lot on Leimert Blvd. two weeks ago, I said to myself: “let me try some of the things.“ I engaged the owner in conversation and found out she was from Piedmont. Who could have known? I selected some dessert crepes. I enjoyed my conversation with the owner and was delighted with the crepes. Kolobok later announced a special dinner for Valentine’s Day. That was all I needed. They offered a set menu and it was sumptuous, to put it mildly. My wife and I ordered two dinners. One was a salmon fillet enveloped by a flaky pastry. The English would be tempted to claim it in the name of Wellington because it is a fish version of Beef Wellington. Not since the days of the old Stagecoach restaurant in downtown San Francisco have I had anything this good. Preparing a Wellington is a very tricky thing and this one was done to perfection. The flaky pastry was perfectly browned. Other ingredients were included which only increased the delectability. The other main course was a large lamb shank braised in Georgian wine and fragrant root vegetables. The meat was delectable and ever so tender. To accompany these main courses were salads which included some smoked salmon. Even though it was a dinner for two, there was enough food to feed at least six. In considering how many people the meal could feed, the price was unbelievably low. Only one thing was missing: It was a take-out meal rather than dining in an elegant imperial dining room. It wasn’t a problem, however. We brought the food home, set the table with some nice China and poured a glass of red wine. Memories of my childhood returned when I saw that Kolobok offers stuffed cabbage. Their version was similar to what my grandmother made. My grandmother’s stuffing was entirely beef and Kolobok’s is a mixture of different meats. For quality, quantity, convenience, and price, Kolobok is a very good bet. Oh, I forgot to tell you… Kolobok is named for Russia’s national fairytale. The character is similar to the gingerbread man. I created my own version. In my version Kolobok is a cute little gourmet who ventures into the forest gathering rare and expensive mushrooms and forest berries. Instead of being eaten by the sly fox, Kolobok prepares a sumptuous dinner for his friends. What could be better? For a future treat, contact Ellen Doren, owner of Kolobok, at kolobokfood@gmail.com. articles.text: When walking through Piedmont it is interesting and fun to recognize, and try to name, the various architectural styles employed in the homes and municipal buildings in town. As we have noted previously, this is in fact a big part of the aesthetic appeal of the place – the opposite of a large tract development all of the same architectural type. There are various reasons why certain styles were (and are) chosen for a building, including response to local climate, geography, material availability, as well as simply preference or architectural fashion. To begin with, because Piedmont lies on latitude 38, the same as the Mediterranean Sea, and because many early California settlers were from that area, it is only natural that the imported culture would include architectural inspiration from the surrounding countries, primarily Spain. Like a culture’s language and art, architecture is constantly evolving, constantly changing. It must, since “new” things like automobiles, appliances and superior construction materials and methods didn’t even exist when the styles we are still emulating first came into use. Although Mission Revival, Spanish Colonial, Spanish Colonial Revival are some of the names given to sub-categories of the Mediterranean Style family, it is well to remember that even the baseline style (“Spanish”) is only a snapshot of an architecture at one point in time, itself derived from previous iterations. Confusing? It can be. Architectural scholars can spot a certain type of detail on a building and know exactly how it fits into the historical timeline, but they often disagree on a number of things, including the various labels. But back to the Mediterranean style. Although the variations share many recognizable characteristics (see photos), they all were, and continue to be, eclectic, meaning they are derived from a range of different sources. Any good work of architecture has a strong consistency between the exterior and interior design. In the Mediterranean styles, this is often reflected in high ceilings, exposed rough- hewn beams, textured plaster walls, and of course the continuation of the employment of arched openings. The floor plans are often L shaped, to form “enclosed” exterior courtyards, patios and terraces.

articles.text: Walter Schey of Piedmont passed away peacefully at home on February 18, 2021, following his beloved wife Monika in death nearly three years to the day. He was 87. Born Walter Martin Schey in Berlin, Germany on April 30, 1933, he was the son of Jewish parents Sigmund and Jenny Schey during the rise of the Third Reich. His father succeeded in getting the family to Russia before emigrating them to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania in 1939. Walt grew up in the Squirrel Hill community of Pittsburgh and attended the Carnegie Institute of Technology (now Carnegie Mellon) where he earned a B.S. in Chemical Engineering in 1955. He served his country as a pilot in the U.S. Air Force and received an honorable discharge in 1963. Upon graduating from the UC Berkeley School of Law in 1961, Walt took a fellowship in Munich where he met his beautiful bride, Monika, and they began a sweet courtship. Monika eventually followed him back to San Francisco, where they were married in 1963 and subsequently moved to Oakland. They relocated to Piedmont in 1975, where they raised two children: Martin (PHS Class of 1988) and Juliet (PHS Class of 1993). Walt had a long and well-rewine, especially in the cherished company of family and friends. He was a life-long reader of spy novels and religiously pored over the weekly Barron’s magazine for investment news as part of his diligent study of the stock market. Weekends often found Walt outside, as he loved to sit in the sun to read. He was a great story-teller, who relished in reciting a mischievous joke and particularly mastered the art of making eloquent toasts. Both children followed in his footsteps into the legal profession. His son Martin joined him in his law practice, forming the Schey & Schey partnership that lasted over 20 years. As Walt and Monika’s children married and started their own families, Walt took great pride in his wonderful children-in-law and five gorgeous grandchildren. Walter is survived by his son Martin and daughter-in-law Shonnon of Piedmont, and their children, Samantha and Connor. He is also survived by daughter Juliet and her husband Michael Meinert of Alamo, along with three children, Robbie, Schey and Molly. Walter is predeceased by his wife, Monika, and his parents. articles.text: Healthcare providers can vaccinate people with comorbidities on March 15 A large, drive-through COVID- 19 vaccination clinic was opened at the Alameda County Fairgrounds in Pleasanton on Wednesday, February 17. The county hopes to offer as many as 1,000 vaccination appointments per day in the coming weeks at this location. The Alameda County Fairgrounds clinic is a joint operation between the county, Stanford Health Care-ValleyCare and Sutter Health. Sutter is opening appointments for patients 65 years and older, while Stanford Health Care– Valleycare has appointments for both senior citizens and healthcare workers. Alameda County is only scheduling appointments at the Fairgrounds for seniors and healthcare workers by invitation. Appointments will be open to other essential workers when “vaccine supply permits,” the county’s website says. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. The county says as many as 5,000 vaccine doses could be administered every day at the Fairgrounds soon. However, issues caused by disastrous winter weather around the nation has limited vaccine supply in California and many other states. “Our goal is to provide broad access to vaccine across the county, and this site is a cornerstone of our planning for the future,” said Kathleen Clanon, the Medical Director for the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency. “We are putting in place an infrastructure that provides immediate access to seniors and essential workers and allows us to scale up quickly if vaccine supply increases.” The Fairgrounds is the second large-scale vaccination operation in Alameda County. On Tuesday, February 16, the Oakland Coliseum opened as a “mega vaccination site,” the first federally funded “supersite” in the United States. On February 8, the county began vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1, as defined by the state’s eligibility framework. This group includes people aged 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. Several teachers and other staff members for the Piedmont Unified School District reported receiving vaccine doses in recent days. This entire phase of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents countywide. People in Tier 1, Phase 1A continue to be vaccinated. This phase, comprised of healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities, was the first group eligible when the first doses arrived in December. In Alameda County, Phase 1A includes an estimated 145,000 people. Both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccine being used in California require patients to receive two doses of vaccine administered several weeks apart. As of Sunday, February 21, the Alameda County Public Health Department reported that 2,736 Piedmonters have received their first dose of the vaccine. Furthermore, 924 Piedmonters have received their second dose and are now fully vaccinated. A total of 319,814 vaccine doses have been administered in Alameda County. Its Public Health Department reported that 79,893 county residents have been fully vaccinated, roughly 5 percent of Alameda County’s population. On Monday, March 15 new state guidance goes into effect that allows healthcare providers to decide whether to vaccinate individuals ages 16 to 64 with certain health conditions that leaves them more at risk to COVID-19 mortality. After Phase 1A, Phase 1B Tier 1 and people with underlying health conditions, the state has said it is moving toward “age-based prioritization” but has not provided many details about who will be eligible after these three groups. Earlier frameworks suggested that vaccination eligibility would widen significantly in the spring, but the state has not released an updated timeline. The state has administered over 7.4 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 8.8 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. Statewide, Phase 1A includes about 3 million people while Phase 1B Tier 1 includes another 12 million.

articles.text: University of California Health (UCH) and the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) are launching an innovative data modeling consortium to ensure public health policy makers have timely, relevant analysis to support pandemic-related decision making. Berkeley Public Health’s Dr. Maya Petersen is co-chair of the new group. Petersen is an associate professor of Biostatistics and Epidemiology and Head of the Division of Biostatistics at Cal. She focuses on the development and application of novel causal inference methods to problems in health and community-based interventions. “Through this collaboration, UC researchers will be able to respond quickly to the needs of public health officials. We’ve not experienced a public health emergency of this intensity in our lifetimes, and this real-time partnership is a very tangible way in which UC is supporting its mission to the people of California,” Petersen said. The modeling consortium is a regular forum in which 150 faculty members across the University of California system, primarily in epidemiology, infectious diseases, economics, statistics, computer science, ecology, and data modeling and statistics, work with CDPH modelers and public health experts to develop information to inform the pandemic response in California. Researchers will use the platform to share results of their ongoing analyses with public health leaders to provide real-time evidence to inform decision-making. Dr. Erica Pan, the State Epidemiologist said “[CDPH’s] ability to leverage the brain-trust of the UC system in addressing critical public health challenges will have far reaching implications beyond COVID-19. This type of partnership will provide the infrastructure and model we need to not only enhance public health action for this pandemic, but for other public health priorities as well.” The group is tasked with accomplishing major legwork in the state’s fight against the current health crisis. UC investigators contributing to the consortium include: • Short-term forecasts of COVID- 19 metrics such as case rates, hospitalizations and intensive care unit occupancy; • Scenario models that quantify the likely impact of various potential public health decisions, as well as vaccine distribution strategies, therapeutic use and adherence to non-pharmaceutical interventions; • Cross-cutting health equity analytics to deepen understanding of COVID-19 disparities throughout the state; and • Economic modeling to answer questions about cost, and overall economic effects of COVID-19, such as the effect of changes to social services and benefits on hospitalizations or deaths. “The UC consortium exemplifies our State’s commitment to using science and evidence to drive our public health decision making. We are very proud to launch this academic and public health consortium. Expanding the engagement with our academic partners will improve the timeliness and relevance of evidence being generated for decision-making and proves that we can meet the challenges of this pandemic, together,” said Dr. Tomas Aragon, Director of the California Department of Public Health and adjunct professor at Berkeley Public Health.
articles.title: UC Health partners with State Dept. of Public Health to accelerate COVID data modeling

This is reflected in the relaxed asymmetry of the design, in both the plans and elevations (generally the more symmetry, the more formal the style). Another clue is the extensive use of inside/outside spaces. The “outdoor rooms” we discussed a few months ago are very common, formed by building walls and arcades, resulting in small patios, and/or large courtyards. These all have a strong connection via large doors with many lites (windows) to the interior rooms. Arched openings of windows, doors, and arcades are pervasive and normally in irregular compositions of various types and shapes, further contributing to the informality of the design. Regardless of the often subtle differences of the various subgroups, this style of architecture is generally a very casual one with warm character, well suited to the climate and attitudes of California and Piedmont. articles.text: Surely you have seen the magnificent stands of Coast Redwoods around Piedmont, but have you noticed the row of seven Dawn Redwoods growing along the back of the former quarry in Dracena Park? Nominated by Lyle Gordon, these beauties were designated as Heritage Trees in 2018. The Dawn Redwood, or Metasequoia glyptostroboides, is a prehistoric tree that was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in 1941 in China. Unlike Coast Redwoods, which are evergreen, Dawn Redwoods are deciduous, and shed leaves annually. They are fast growing and have delicate, feathery leaves, and distinctive, rounded cones. These trees are a wonderful part of Piedmont’s urban forest and worth seeking out on a walk or Dawn Redwoods are known for their distinctive, rounded cones. You can read the fascinating story of the rediscovery of the Dawn Redwood at https:// landscapearchitecturemagazine.org/2016/01/19/the-metasequoia-mystery/. The Piedmont Park Commission is now accepting nominations for 2021 Heritage Trees through March 19. To nominate a tree, visit the City’s website, http://www.ci.piedmont.ca.us/ and complete the downloadable form. The trees selected this year will be recognized at the annual Arbor Day virtual celebration on April 30. For more information, contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont. ca.gov, or 510-420-3064. Piedmont’s Heritage Trees: Dracena Park’s Dawn Redwoods By Amber Brumfiel Surely you have seen the magnificent stands of Coast Redwoods around Piedmont, but have you noticed the row of seven Dawn Redwoods growing along the back of the former quarry in Dracena Park? Nominated by Lyle Gordon, these beauties were designated as Heritage Trees in 2018. The Dawn Redwood, or Metasequoia glyptostroboides, is a prehistoric tree that was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in 1941 in China. Unlike Coast Redwoods, which are evergreen, Dawn Redwoods are deciduous, and shed leaves annually. They are fast growing and have delicate, feathery leaves, and distinctive, rounded cones.
